text:
# Uttaramēghaḥ |

Of women with divided hair <note>a reference to the practice of parting the hair as a sign of being a wife</note>. "A woman with a part in her hair is a bride" <note>original: 'nārī sīmantinī vadhūḥ'</note>, says the <term>Amara</term> <gloss>Amara-kośa, a standard Sanskrit thesaurus</gloss>. [Brought by a friend] Brought near or obtained through a friend. The word "friend" <term>suhṛt</term> is used to remove doubts regarding separation. News of the lover is the "lover's tidings" <term>kāntōdantaḥ</term>. "Tidings, occurrences, reports, and news are <term>udanta</term>" <note>original: 'vārtā pravṛttirvṛttānta udantaḥ syāt'</note>, says the <term>Amara</term>. The meaning is that it is almost as joyful as a meeting, or contact with the lover, though slightly less than the actual event.

Now he gives the message—

"O long-lived one, at my request and for your own benefit,
Speak thus to her, your companion, who dwells in the hermitage of Ramagiri:
'I am alive and well, though separated from you, and I ask after your welfare, O helpless one;
For those in distress, this is the first thing to be said.'" <41>

"To her" <note>referring to the beloved</note>. "O long-lived one" <term>āyuṣman</term>. The suffix <term>matup</term> <gloss>denoting possession</gloss> is used here for praise, meaning one whose life is worthy because of the benefit done to others. "At my request" <term>mama vacanāt</term>, meaning a request for a favor, "and for your own benefit," meaning to fulfill yourself through the act of helping others. Even though the act of helping is the object of the action, the genitive case <term>ātmanaḥ</term> is not contradictory when intending a relationship, as in "he does a favor for himself." As the poet <term>Bhāravi</term> says: "That is wealth, through which one does a favor to others." Likewise, <term>Śrīharṣa</term> says: "To do a favor to the good, to see wealth, to go through the sky." Thus, the statement of the teacher <term>Nātha</term>—"sometimes, because of the observation of a second, everything is as such"—is a statement of necessity. Speak thus to that beloved. What should you say? "O helpless one, your companion, your husband, dwells in the hermitages of Ramagiri, the mountain of paintings. I am not dead." He provides the reason for being alive: "Being separated from you and suffering, I ask about your welfare." Because of the state of distress, the verb "to ask" <term>pṛcchati</term> takes two objects. Indeed, for living beings who are prone to sudden misfortune, this greeting is the very first thing that must be asked. The suffix <term>ṇyat</term> is used in the sense of necessity.

"With a body, a very thin body pressed against a thin body;
With eyes full of tears, and an unrestrained longing for one who is longing;"

<note>1. Long-lived one. 2. You should speak. 3. One. 4. Separated from you, appointed. 5. This is the first thing to be asked for beings prone to misfortune; this is the first greeting for those whose means are decaying. 6. O slender one, and thin. 7. With liquid tears.</note>

<summary>The Yaksha instructs the cloud to convey a message of health and longing to his wife, emphasizing that asking after the welfare of the other is the first duty of those separated by misfortune.</summary>
<keywords>Ramagiri, message, longing, separation, welfare, duty, Yaksha, messenger</keywords>
